trajectory_summary: This is a calm, procedurally solid call: the rep skips a bill-anchor entirely (there is none to anchor — customer doesn't have Virginia utility data yet) and instead builds the appointment around verified address/roof/title/utility/credit facts, flexing scheduling twice to fit the customer's real move timeline. The rep misses two threads that would have made the call sharper — the customer's opening discomfort about his number being shared, and the wife being on title without being pulled into the follow-up call — but neither wrecks the outcome. The appointment is booked with a specific day and time, though the spouse's absence from that booking is a real structural gap the closer needs to know about.

bill_document_audit.reasoning: Rep never raised getting a utility bill in any form; instead he substituted square footage and a Zillow lookup as the design proxy since the customer hasn't moved in yet and has no bill history at the new address.

The rep acknowledged the design request generally but never explicitly reinforced this specific cost-of-electricity motivation later in the call or at booking.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: spouse-on-title not included in booked appointment
primary_coaching_focus.quote: Well, my wife is just you know, we're both on the on the on the mortgage and title, etcetera.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer confirmed a co-owner on title, which per protocols.spouse_decision should trigger explicit inclusion of the spouse on the specialist call; instead the appointment was booked for the customer alone, leaving the appointment structurally vulnerable to a stalled decision at proposal stage.

key_moments.quote: I I was trying to get an estimate just to see, like, how much and I figured the website would give me, I didn't know it was gonna, like, form my phone numbers to, like, you know
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a soft trust-or-scam signal at the very top of the call — the customer is uneasy about how a web form turned into his number being called. The rep never acknowledges it; he proceeds straight into the Tesla-adjacent Ion intro and the pitch. This is the same concern that resurfaces at 06:35 about unknown callers, so leaving it unaddressed here let it ride unresolved through the whole call.

key_moments.quote: I'm moving I'm military, so I'm moving to Virginia.
key_moments.stewart_read: A permanent-change-of-station disclosure is a meaningful life-transition detail — new home, new state, family relocating separately from him — but the rep's next line goes straight to the mechanics of the design ('we can definitely still show your design... based off the square footage') without any acknowledgment of the move itself beyond a later 'congratulations on the new home.' It's not a harsh miss, but the vulnerability_disclosure principle calls for a specific acknowledgment before bridging to value, and here the bridge happens with no acknowledgment at all.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. We I mean, we can definitely still show your design. Again, that's just to make it a little bit more accurate, but we can still take a look at it based off, like, the square footage and everything like that.
key_moments.stewart_read: Facing a customer with zero bill data (he hasn't moved yet), the rep pivots cleanly to square footage as the qualifying proxy instead of stalling on the missing bill_anchoring step. This is the correct adaptive move for a genuinely non-standard scenario (pre-move, no utility history) rather than a scripted failure.

key_moments.quote: And then, is there any good is there gonna be anybody else with title with you when you close on Friday?
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep asks the co-owner question correctly and gets a clear answer — wife is on the mortgage and title — but never comes back to make sure she's included on the follow-up specialist call. The appointment is booked for the customer alone.
